items.title: Richard Powell Unsettles Race and Color Theory
items.author: Lowery Sims
items.summary: Drawing on the work of artists and theorists alike, the art historian traces how generations of Black painters have deployed color and how color, in turn, shapes our understanding of Blackness.

images.caption: Lámina de Hyperallergic
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Lowery Sims
Richard Powell Unsettles Race and Color Theory

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Sometime in the 1980s, when I was still a fledgling curator of 20th-century art at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, I was invited to the studio of a rather prominent artist. During our conversation, the work of Jacob Lawrence came up somehow, and the artist mentioned that he was impressed by what he described as Lawrence’s use of “Black” colors. Did I mention this artist was White? 

I was gobsmacked by the comment. Not that I wasn’t attuned to stereotypical societal associations of color — most notably, of bright, loud colors with Black people. In the 1950s, a full three decades before Nancy Reagan practically made red her official color, my Aunt Ruth was appalled that my mother made red coats for my sister and me, rather than using more acceptable pastel colors. Then a friend who grew up in Northern Ireland told me that Protestant Irish factions associated Catholic Irish with loud and bright colors. 

But how did such racially associative ideas translate to the realm of the so-called “fine” arts? I was aware of the place of color theory in the practice of art and knew the names of important theorists, from Johann Wolfgang von Goethe to Johannes Itten to Josef Albers. But otherwise, I presumed artists’ palettes were the result of personal predilection, technical explorations (i.e., the opening up of brushstrokes and form in the 19th century and the introduction of a wall of color in the 20th century), or cultural orientation. So it was therefore with great interest that I approached reading Richard Powell’s latest publication, Colorstruck!: Painting, Pigment, Affect (2026).

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Do scientists have anything left to do in the AI world? More than ever

And even when the external world has granted all it can, there still remain the searchings of the mind and the longings of the heart.

As the world attempts to bring artificial intelligence into focus, it is hard to think of a modern scientific project with a wider range of implications for the future. Some hold that AI has already reached its maximum capabilities , while others maintain that we stand at the beginning of an exponentially expanding demigod , a singularity, the point beyond which it will be impossible for humans to comprehend the accelerating insights of a “super intelligence.”

If the more radical proposition holds, that a singularity is afoot, then the assumption is that everything we do, and even things we cannot dream of, will soon be done by machines. For science, this means that the utilitarian problems we seek to solve will be solved at ever faster rates by machines. What does this mean for scientists? Will there be anything left to do, or are scientists out of jobs?

Astrobiologists must confront a similar thought that is discouraging for people who have dedicated their lives to discovery: What if an alien civilization somewhere out there has already come to know all the mysteries we hope to discover? More poignantly, what if such a species landed on our planet with all of their knowledge in hand (or in tentacle, or in ever-shifting amorphous goo)?

Well, there would be quite a lot of work to do. Communication with such a creature would be a challenge in itself. After that, considerable effort would be required to learn what they know. Such learning might proceed in stages and might take generations. There might be types of knowledge that do not overlap with ours for cultural and philosophical reasons, and we would need to debate the meaning of such differences with ourselves and perhaps with them. Our lives would be anything but boring, and the amount of interesting work to do might even expand.

Many AI researchers think that such an alien is about to land on, or rather grow out of, our planet. An intelligence that is alien both by virtue of the vastness of its knowledge base and the incomprehensibility of its solutions. Many assume that such a creature will rapidly eliminate the need for scientists, but this presumption focuses only on the utilitarian aspects of science—the idea that science is about producing solutions that are useful to society, typically expressed in economic terms.

Indeed, science triumphed in its utility as it contributed to medicine, a greater abundance of crops, aerospace transportation, digital computers, the internet, magnetic resonance imaging, and, perhaps, large language models. All perfectly adhering to the “ Endless Frontier ” predicted in postwar America. Utilitarianism is a good reason to invest in science, but it is shaky ground for a deep philosophy about the meaning of science. Technology is largely about optimizing on a task, science seeks something deeper, and this is often the pursuit of understanding, whose long-term benefits are impossible to predict. Even with tools in hand, such as AI, our focus should be on the challenge and meaning of engaging in tool-assisted activities as human beings. Consider the board games chess and Go, the marathon, and the mechanical watch.

In 1997, Deep Blue played, and beat, Garry Kasparov, widely considered one of the greatest players the game has known. In 2016, AlphaGo defeated Lee Sedol , the strongest Go player the world had ever seen. By 2017, AlphaZero had taught itself in nine hours to play chess at a level no human will ever match. The outcome was not the collapse of chess. On the contrary, more people play chess now than at any point in its history. Chess.com surpassed 150 million members in the post-AlphaZero era, and over-the-board tournament participation has grown in parallel. Top grandmasters now study with game engines, and tellingly, the engines have become coaches rather than replacements. The grandmaster’s relationship with the chess engine sharpened the grandmaster’s game, rather than retire the player. The moves played in human tournaments are the player’s own, and the game’s meaning is that of the players, not of the silicon that has long since outclassed them.

The fastest car in the world, the Bugatti Chiron, can complete the 26.2 miles of a marathon in around 12 minutes. Near-superhuman world record holder Sebastian Sawe, who completed the London Marathon in 1 hour, 59 minutes, and 30 seconds, is ten times slower than the car. No one watching Sawe would conclude that the car is faster than humans. The marathon was never a means of transport. It is a challenge to the body, and the physiological question is, how far can we push the flesh before it fails?

Seiko introduced the first quartz watch in 1969. The Seiko Astron was accurate to within a few seconds per month, far more accurate than any mechanical watch of the time. The mechanical watch was on the verge of extinction, and the Swiss watch industry was decimated by the so-called “quartz crisis” of the 1970s. However, the industry survived and flourished by creating ever more complex and ingenious mechanical timepieces. The tourbillon, for example, was invented in 1795 to compensate for gravity in pocket watches. Today, there are many wristwatches with a tourbillon that serve no purpose other than to demonstrate the skills of the watchmaker.

The pattern discernible across these three examples is a transition from the belief that utility is the unique metric of progress to the deeper understanding that what we care about is craft and meaning. The utility of the activity might have been an original focus, but people came to realize that what they more profoundly cared about was the craft, style, and meaning of the activity. And mastering the activity was measured against the tradition in which one was practicing. And from this constellation of craft, style, and meaning derives the very practical principles of curiosity, search, and abduction, from which truly novel discovery derives.

And similar epistemic disruption has already occurred in history. The separation of natural philosophy into natural science and philosophy, which can be compared with the breakup of the Beatles, the forced exile of Romeo from Verona, or the disintegration of the 1997–98 Chicago Bulls.

Scientists might say that we no longer need to be mystified by matter, as we can measure it, we can have theories about it, and we can even make predictions about it. Yet philosophers are not deterred by this progress, many new details and measurements which science has provided, have opened new territory for philosophy, making the philosophical problems of the nature of matter and the universe more expansive. Thus, for example, the strangeness of quantum mechanics led to so many deep philosophical questions that the physicists started to tell each other to “shut up and calculate” and to stop worrying about the strangeness of the quantum world and instead to use the mathematical tools of quantum mechanics. But the philosophers, of course, have continued to ponder over the problems of quantum mechanics, to the point of making quantum foundations an important part of fundamental physics.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
In the wee hours of a busy Saturday morning, on June 28, 1969, police raided The Stonewall Inn in Manhattan’s Greenwich Village, a renowned hangout for the LGBTQ+ community. During the 1950s and 1960s, few businesses openly welcomed gay people, and the legal system was against them—even two consenting adults in the privacy of their own home could face years in prison or a psychiatric institution if convicted of the crime of sodomy. Bar raids were common, but this one was particularly fraught due to the volume of people, and police quickly lost control. A riot erupted, which sparked even further protests over the coming weeks in what became known as the Stonewall uprising.

Among those on the front lines, from the raid onward, was Marsha P. Johnson—the “P” stands for Pay It No Mind—a Black transgender woman who advocated throughout the 1960s and 1970s for gay and transgender rights, LGBTQ+ youth, and those affected by HIV and AIDS. Known fondly as The Saint of Christopher Street, nodding to the well-known and welcoming area for the gay community (and home of The Stonewall Inn), she was widely known for her effervescent smile, creative clothing, and the flowers she would often wear in her hair.

For quilter Rosy Petri, Johnson proved a beautiful and vibrant personality for a large-scale textile work in We’re Still Here: Quilted Works Curated by Carolyn Mazloomi at Claire Oliver Gallery.

The works of 15 contemporary quilt artists take center stage in the expansive group exhibition. The show emphasizes work created by members of the Women of Color Quilters Network (WCQN), which historian, curator, and quilter Carolyn Mazloomi founded in 1985. Boldly pictorial and incorporating a wide range of materials, the pieces in We’re Still Here transcend the definition of quilts as stitched bed coverings; the compositions are rooted in the timeless craft of piecing and sewing, yet their portraits, stories, and collages surge into the realm of art.

L’Merchie Frazier’s “Climate Change in my Head: Afro Future Still Here,” for example, adopts a watercolor-like appearance with layers of nylon. Like many works in the show, a crucial topic is rendered front-and-center. Alita Aldridge’s “Underground Takes a Village” reflects the cooperation needed to make the Underground Railroad viable for enslaved people seeking freedom. And April Anue Shipp’s “The Oracle of Liberation” depicts abolitionist Frederick Douglass holding red and blue pills—a reference to the 1999 film The Matrix—in which we’re presented with a choice between seeing reality for what it is or remaining ignorant.

In addition to history, Black community, family, and other themes, bold portraiture recurs throughout the exhibition, such as in Viola Burley Leak’s “Maya Angelou II.” The renowned writer and civil rights activist peers over symbolic representations of her life’s work, including a bird fleeing an enclosure in a nod to her seminal memoir, I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings.

“All of the work I make, and the work of my fellow quilters, deals with Black history and material culture,” Mazloomi says in a statement. Through WCQN, along with curatorial projects and in advocacy of the art form, she strives to raise critical awareness of Black quilters’ practices. “This exhibition is our way of saying that our history cannot be erased by any politician or revisionist force; our work will always showcase our triumphs, suffering, creativity, courage, bravery, and genius of my people. Black history is American history.”

We’re Still Here continues through January 7 in Harlem. You might also enjoy Chronicle Books’ recent release, Stories in the Seams: A People’s History of Black Quilts and Their Makers.

items.title: This Self-Charging Toothbrush Has Bristles That Generate Electricity to Help Kill Bacteria That Cause Cavities and Gum Disease
items.author: Smithsonian Smart News
items.summary: In a short clinical trial, participants who used the experimental toothbrush reported less plaque, gum inflammation and bleeding than those who used traditional nylon-bristled brushes. However, more research is required to assess the tool's safety and efficacy

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Researchers in China have reinvented a familiar tool: the toothbrush.

Brushing your teeth is an important part of your oral care routine. Both regular and electric toothbrushes rely on physically scrubbing away bacteria that can cause cavities and gum disease. But a new design, described November 4 in the journal Science Advances , features bristles that generate bacteria-killing electricity when they bend, perhaps providing a long-awaited update to the hygiene tool.

“Toothbrushes have undergone no substantive improvements beyond their mechanical function for about 1118 years to date,” the researchers write in the study. “Conventional toothbrushes often fail to establish an antibacterial environment on the tooth surface, allowing bacteria to recover and recolonize. Here, we developed an innovative self-charged toothbrush that integrates daily tooth brushing with piezoelectric functionality.”

Piezoelectric materials generate electricity when put under mechanical stress, like being squeezed or compressed. In the new study, researchers applied this property to the toothbrush by creating bristles from polyvinylidene fluoride, a material that produces an electrical charge when it bends.

The electricity doesn’t directly zap oral bacteria, however. Instead, the charge creates highly unstable molecules called reactive oxygen species in the saliva. These molecules disrupt the membranes of bacteria in dental plaque —a sticky layer of the harmful organisms, along with food particles and spit.

“The concept is great,” Nicholas Jakubovics , an oral microbiologist at Newcastle University in England who did not participate in the research, tells New Scientist ’s Christa Lesté-Lasserre. “Basically, the mechanical forces recharge the surface, so it’s really innovative. Anything that even slightly improves the way dental care works could have a benefit, because oral disease is just so widespread.” Experts estimate that almost 3.7 billion people worldwide have oral diseases , such as gum disease and tooth decay.

The researchers first conducted lab tests of the piezoelectric toothbrush using two key oral pathogens: Streptococcus mutans , which causes cavities, and Porphyromonas gingivalis , which causes gum disease. The charge-producing bristles killed about half of the cavity-causing bacteria and more than half of the gum disease agent present, while traditional nylon bristles eliminated only about 9 percent and 8 percent, respectively.

Then, they moved to a human trial. The team enrolled 115 participants with tooth decay or mild gum disease, called gingivitis. They asked some people to use the electricity-generating toothbrushes and others to use nylon-bristled brushes twice a day for three months.

At the end of the study period, participants who brushed with the experimental tool had less plaque, gum inflammation and bleeding than regular toothbrush users, the team found.

Early forms of toothbrushes, such as a “chew stick” with a frayed end, have existed since 3,000 B.C.E .

“It’s great to have new approaches that actually enhance the effect of mechanical cleaning,” Jakubovics tells Live Science ’s Isha Ishtiaq. “The idea that the toothbrush surface itself is actively doing something is really interesting.”

One of the limits of the research, however, is the clinical trial’s short duration, he notes. “We would want to make sure that it is safe on the tissues for long-term use.”

Frank Scannapieco , a periodontist and microbiologist at the University of Buffalo who did not participate in the study, agrees that more research is necessary to prove the toothbrush is safe and effective, per Nature ’s Elizabeth Gibney.

This isn’t the first time researchers have taken a swing at upgrading toothbrushes. Previous designs have included bristles with antibacterial chemicals, but researchers aren’t sure if they have a lasting effect. Others produced charged particles to help clean teeth, but these require batteries.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
What does it mean to give art the time and attention it requires? Since its founding in 1964, the New York Studio School (NYSS) has pursued this question through an approach to art education grounded in sustained studio practice, rigorous inquiry, and the conviction that artists develop through the ongoing process of making, looking, and thinking. 

Located at 8 West 8th Street in Greenwich Village, the School occupies a building with a rich history in American art. Founded by artist and educator Mercedes Matter, NYSS carries forward a tradition of independent thinking and experimentation, offering an environment where artists can challenge assumptions, investigate fundamental questions, and develop their work through direct engagement with materials and ideas.

The School’s full-time, two-year Master of Fine Arts (MFA) program is a 60-credit degree centered on intensive, individual studio practice in drawing, painting, sculpture, and art history. Rather than prescribing a single artistic direction, the program provides students with the time, space, and mentorship to pursue their own questions and cultivate their own distinctive artistic language. 

At the heart of the New York Studio School MFA program is the relationship between individual practice and collective exchange. Students are assigned private or semi-private studio spaces and select two core faculty artists to serve as their atelier mentors. Through studio visits, group critiques, and ongoing dialogue with faculty and peers, students are encouraged to examine their work from multiple perspectives while developing the confidence and critical awareness to move their practice forward. 

The curriculum combines independent studio work with intensive two-week Marathons, drawing courses, Critical Studies seminars, and encounters with visiting artists. The School’s renowned Evening Lecture Series and Exhibitions further connect students to a broad community of artists, writers, historians, and thinkers. Drawing remains a foundational component of the program, informing the study of painting and sculpture and encouraging deeper attention to perception, form, space, and material. 

Students in the MFA program are encouraged to engage with the histories of art while questioning established conventions, exploring the relationships between representation and abstraction, and discovering new possibilities through sustained experimentation. The goal is to support the development of an independent, thoughtful, and resilient artistic practice. The MFA program’s second year culminates with a thesis project and exhibition in the School’s historic galleries, connecting a new generation of artists with a building that has been part of New York’s cultural life for more than a century.

For artists seeking a demanding, immersive environment in which to deepen their work, the New York Studio School offers an education built around the essential questions of art-making, and the time, community, and commitment needed to pursue them.

items.title: This Philosopher Was One of the First People to Donate His Body to Science. Nearly 200 Years Later, Researchers Are Still Learning From It
items.author: Smithsonian Smart News
items.summary: Jeremy Bentham, the founder of utilitarianism, had his corpse publicly dissected and turned into an "auto-icon," a lifelike display featuring his skeleton dressed in one of his suits

images.caption: Imagen principal de Smithsonian Smart News
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Sarah Kuta
YouTube Logo

videos.caption: Enlace audiovisual citado en la nota

items.cleanReaderHtml:
As a young man, English philosopher Jeremy Bentham vowed to donate his body to science, becoming one of the first people on record to make such a declaration. And he made good on his promise. After Bentham died at age 84, his remains were publicly dissected, then transformed into an “ auto-icon ”—a lifelike display featuring his skeleton dressed in one of his suits, which has been preserved by the University College London (UCL) ever since.

Now, nearly two centuries later, Bentham’s body is still yielding new scientific insights.

UCL researchers recently revisited Bentham’s remains, using computed tomography (CT) scanning to create a detailed, 3D model of his mummified head. They share the process and their findings in a short film called Bentham Revealed .

Born in 1748 in London, Bentham was a precocious child who enrolled at Oxford University at just 12 years old. Though he trained as a lawyer, he ultimately devoted his life to philosophy and writing. Bentham became best known as the founder of utilitarianism , a philosophy built around the idea that the best actions are those that produce the greatest happiness for the greatest number of people.

He applied this principle to a wide range of issues, advocating for prison reform , animal welfare , women’s rights , the decriminalization of homosexuality and the abolition of slavery—positions that were considered radical in 18th- and 19th-century Britain. His ideas inspired the founding of UCL, which opened to students in 1826.

But perhaps Bentham’s most radical act was his decision to donate his body to science. In his will, he bequeathed his corpse to his friend, British physician Thomas Southwood Smith , and asked him to arrange a public dissection of his body. Smith obliged, tasking anatomist Richard Dugard Grainger with carrying out the procedure five days after Bentham’s death in June 1832, according to a university statement . Smith then created the auto-icon, which he kept at his house until 1850, when he donated it to UCL. It’s currently on view at UCL’s student center.

Bentham coined the term auto-icon himself, defining it as “self image” or “self representation.” He hoped to inspire others to follow suit. “He imagined a future where people were making auto-icons to keep their dead relatives around,” Tannis Davidson , who led the recent research and serves as a curator at UCL's Grant Museum of Zoology, tells Live Science ’s Tom Metcalfe.

Smith tried to preserve Bentham’s head for the auto-icon, but his efforts ultimately failed, leading him to commission a wax replica instead. Bentham’s real head was displayed at the feet of the auto-icon for years, until it was stolen and held ransom for several days in 1975. After that, it was stashed away for safe keeping.

Bentham requested that his head be preserved in “the New Zealand manner.” He was referring to the preserved heads, or mokomokai , of the Māori, New Zealand’s indigenous inhabitants.

Bentham’s head is still used for research today. The team’s recent CT scans revealed that Bentham was missing several teeth and had advanced arthritis in his lower jaw, which likely caused excruciating pain. His tooth problems aren’t particularly surprising, given that the importance of regular dental hygiene was not yet widely understood. “Dentistry 200 years ago was a very different kettle of fish than it is today,” Davidson tells Live Science .

It’s not clear whether Bentham knew about the arthritis in his jaw, but he was fully aware of his dental issues. He confided in an 1830 letter that he had “never been fond of having my teeth [extracted], but I have more than once submitted to the momentary torment to rid myself of the enduring one.” Bentham also described some of his home remedies, writing in another 1830 letter about heating a knitting needle, then applying it directly to an exposed nerve.

The recent investigation also sheds light on Smith’s attempts to preserve Bentham’s head for the auto-icon. He appears to have removed most of Bentham’s brain, but he left behind some of the dura mater, the thick, outermost membrane. Additionally, he drilled a hole through the top of Bentham’s skull, which was meant to attach it to the auto-icon using a metal rod. Smith also added highly detailed glass eyes—complete with an anatomically correct optic nerve—to the preserved head.

One of the team’s primary goals was to learn more about the mummification process, according to Bentham Revealed . They also hoped the CT imagery might serve as a baseline for monitoring the head’s condition over time and determining how best to preserve it.

But, beyond that, they say the model of Bentham’s head could prove useful to a wide range of professionals, from healthcare providers and archaeologists to museum specialists. For example, a 3D-printed replica of Bentham’s skull could one day support teaching, research and conservation efforts.

items.title: The North Atlantic Right Whale Population Has Shrunk, Raising Concerns About the Future of the Critically Endangered Species
items.author: Smithsonian Smart News
items.summary: The massive marine mammals are dying from ship strikes, fishing gear entanglements and other causes, which is affecting the species' ability to grow its numbers. The animals were hunted to the brink of extinction around 100 years ago

images.caption: Imagen principal de Smithsonian Smart News
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Sarah Kuta
Two scientists on a boat with the ocean in the background

items.cleanReaderHtml:
The North Atlantic right whale population shrank slightly in 2025, raising concerns about the future of the critically endangered species.

Scientists counted 382 individuals last year, according to new numbers released this week by the North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium. That’s a 1.8 percent decrease from the 2024 estimate of 389 whales.

Meanwhile, the number of reproductive females held steady at 73, according to the consortium, which is made up of scientists from the New England Aquarium’s Anderson Cabot Center for Ocean Life and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

North Atlantic right whales are massive marine mammals that can weigh as much as 140,000 pounds. They spend their winters in the shallow waters off North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia and Florida, where they give birth and raise their calves. Then, they swim more than 1,000 miles north to spend the spring, summer and fall feeding in the food-rich waters off New England and Canada.

They’re one of three species of right whales, along with the North Pacific right whale and the Southern right whale . All three species are what’s known as filter feeders, meaning they use their baleen —flexible, comb-like plates that hang from their upper jaws—to tiny creatures called copepods from the water.

Commercial whalers hunted right whales to the brink of extinction by the late 19th and early 20th centuries, dubbing them the “right” whales to go after because they were relatively easy to kill and retrieve.

All three species have been protected under the U.S. Endangered Species Act since 1970. Still, the colossal creatures have been slow to recover—and their populations remain small today. Right whales can die or suffer life-threatening injuries after being struck by boats or becoming tangled in fishing gear.

“Imagine if you were wrapped in rope that moved as you moved … literally sawing into your body,” Philip Hamilton , a biologist with the New England Aquarium, tells CBC News ’ Leila Beaudoin. “It is really painful. They don’t have arms. The pain is … kind of unimaginable.”

Climate change, noise pollution and oil and gas development also threaten the whales. Rising ocean temperatures are particularly dangerous for the massive animals. As the North Atlantic heats up, copepods are moving toward cooler waters, prompting the whales to follow them into areas where they’re not protected from ship strikes and entanglements.

“We know that this population can and will move around to find food, and if we aren’t protecting them throughout their range, we may see another situation where we have this tremendous decline again,” Heather Pettis , chair of the North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium and a biologist at the New England Aquarium, tells Patrick Whittle of the Associated Press .

Over the past decade, North Atlantic right whales have been experiencing high rates of deaths and serious injuries, a period NOAA has dubbed an “ unusual mortality event .” The primary causes have been vessel strikes and entanglements, with 177 total individuals getting killed or injured between 2017 and 2026. The true number is likely higher, as NOAA notes that only about a third of right whale deaths are recorded.

The deaths are affecting the species’ ability to grow its numbers. The 2025 population estimate is 20 percent lower than the high of 483 in 2011, according to the consortium.

Southern right whales are also struggling. Hundreds of calves have washed up dead along Argentina's coast in recent months, likely due to a bacterium that can cause skin infections.

Scientists and conservationists are calling for stronger protections to prevent North Atlantic right whales from disappearing, including stricter vessel speed limits and measures to reduce entanglements in commercial fishing gear. “Right whales cannot afford to wait any longer,” Pettis says in the statement.

items.author: Philip Ball
items.summary: How the great scientist’s thought experiment in the 19th century, which reconciled God and physics, remains vital in science today The post The Everlasting Life of Maxwell’s Demon appeared first on Nautilus .

items.cleanReaderHtml:
How the great scientist’s thought experiment in the 19th century, which reconciled God and physics, remains vital in science today

James Clerk Maxwell had good reason to feel contented in 1867. That year the Scottish physicist explained how the properties of gases derive from the frenetic motions of their inscrutable molecular particles. Two years earlier he had published a theory that united electricity and magnetism, one of the supreme achievements of 19th-century science, and a foundational law of physics. Maxwell had even made the first-ever proper color photograph. He was arguably the most distinguished physical scientist in Great Britain. But something deep in the laws of physics was troubling him. To get around it, Maxwell enlisted the help of a demon.

The problem was the second law of thermodynamics. It was inferred in the mid-19th century by the German physicist Rudolf Clausius. In Clausius’s formulation, the second law insisted that heat can never spontaneously pass from a cold substance to a hotter one. This is what we know intuitively: Hot coffee always cools, but cold coffee never spontaneously gets hot again.

This story is from “The Hot Issue,” the latest from Nautilus . To get it in print, join by Nov 30 .

Clausius’ contemporaries were alarmed by what his second law implies. If heat is always passing from hot to cold, this means that all concentrations of heat are gradually dissipated and become a uniform thermal buzz in the background: Everything ends up at the same temperature. There must come a time when this is all there is. All pockets of energy will be dissipated, and no further change of any consequence can happen. The Scottish-Irish scientist William Thomson (later made Lord Kelvin) called this the heat death of the universe—not, as the name might imply, an infernal conflagration, but on the contrary an anticlimactic running down of everything.

The dreary end of all things may be a long way off, but for a devout Christian like Maxwell, the remoteness was no consolation. He believed in the eternal life promised by the scriptures. But he was also too much the scientist to accept that Christian doctrine could conflict with physical laws. And what about human free will, the means by which individuals could seek salvation? What could that mean in a world enslaved by the second law?

Theories in physiology then made the world and human behavior seem deterministic and inevitable, says historian of science Matthew Stanley of New York University, author of Huxley’s Church and Maxwell’s Demon . Maxwell, says Stanley, “was trying to figure out how there could be a ‘hole’ in theories that allowed for free will without giving up on laws of physics.” Stanley points out there was no great schism between theistic scientists like Maxwell and naturalists who saw no need for God’s involvement in the running of the universe. Both believed in natural laws like the second law and Isaac Newton’s laws of motion, and devout believers tended to feel sure these could be reconciled with an omnipotent God.

In 1867, Maxwell set about looking for a loophole that might safeguard his faith. He wrote to his friend Peter Guthrie Tait, who was preparing a book on thermo-dynamics, to say that he believed he had found one. In the “kinetic theory of gases” that Maxwell had just developed, the properties of gases—such as the fact that their pressure is proportional to their temperature—could be understood within a “microscopic” picture that considered the motions of the component molecules.

In this view, hotter gases have higher-energy and faster molecules on average than colder ones—but there is always a statistical spread of energies. If, Maxwell argued, you could measure the number of molecules with different energies in a gas at any given temperature, the graph would look like a sort of bell curve. If we raise the temperature of the gas, the peak of the bell curve shifts to higher energies, but also the hump itself flattens and broadens.

This, at any rate, is how things would look for a gas with an equal temperature everywhere—a gas at thermal equilibrium. But there’s not a lot you can do with a gas like that. If, on the other hand, you have a gas that is hotter in one region than another—if it’s out of equilibrium—you can extract useful work from it. The hotter region will have a higher pressure, and so it could push a piston into the colder region, driving some kind of engine. That was the basis of the steam engines of the Industrial Revolution, which had prompted the invention of the science of thermo-dynamics to predict and hopefully improve the efficiency of such devices.

But there is a bitter truth to the second law: It works to smooth away any such useful differences in temperature. In a gas with a hot region, the more energetic molecules will inevitably get spread out among the less energetic ones until energy is, on average, spread evenly. It’s just like stirring the cream in your coffee: The two will inevitably mix.

Once that has happened, there’s no going back. You can’t unstir the coffee. There is no physical law which says that the reverse is impossible—the chance that all the hotter molecules in a room might, just by chance, congregate in a hot cluster in one corner is not zero. But the chances of that happening are so astronomically small that it might as well be.

To defeat the second law, Maxwell needed to find some way of marshaling gas molecules so that the normal tendency for hot and cold regions to equalize would be reversed. If you could arrange for that, you could harness the temperature difference to do useful work. For this seemingly miraculous feat, the Christian physicist summoned a demon.

In truth, Maxwell himself never called it that. Heaven forbid! In his letter to Tait, he merely postulated a “finite being”—an “intelligent being endowed with free will”—small enough to “see” each molecule of the gas and able to keep track of it. When Thomson later mischievously dubbed this entity a demon, Maxwell grumbled to Tait: “Call him no more a demon but a valve.”

items.author: David Nield
items.summary: The survival of the species depends on it The post For the First Time, This Dazzling San Francisco Snake is Being Released Into the Wild appeared first on Nautilus .

items.cleanReaderHtml:
The distinctive-looking San Francisco garter snake ( Thamnophis sirtalis tetrataenia ) lives a perilous existence. Only a few thousand remain across San Mateo and Santa Cruz, and the species has been on the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s endangered list since 1967 (the year the list originated).

But there’s new hope for the long-term survival of the species after 62 snakes were released into the wild from the San Francisco Zoo. It’s the first time that San Francisco garter snakes bred in captivity have been placed back into their natural habitat. The hope is that the reptiles will become self-sustaining.

Read more: “ This Snake’s Tail Has a Fake ‘Spider’ at the Tip ”

The approach is known as head-starting, where animals are born in a zoo or another managed conservation environment, protected when they’re at their most vulnerable stages of development, and then rewilded at an early age. Experts were strategic at picking the spots in San Francisco most in need of a fresh influx of young garter snakes, both in terms of population numbers and genetic diversity.

“This is an extraordinary accomplishment for everyone who has worked for generations to protect this remarkable species,” biologist Karine Tokatlian, from the Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District, said in a statement . “Seeing these young snakes returning to the wild represents years of research, collaboration, habitat restoration and careful conservation work.”

The story of why the San Francisco garter snake is under such acute threat is a familiar one: Their habitat is disappearing. The living conditions the species relies on are very specific: They need ponds or other bodies of freshwater to find food, plus hillsides for basking and mating as well as rodent burrows for taking cover in the winter.

That particular mix is rarer than ever due to human development, and most suitable sites for the snake are now on private land. Case in point: The largest population is currently in a protected site close to San Francisco International Airport.

Drought, disease, invasive species, and illegal poaching have also put San Francisco garter snake numbers at critically low levels, making the zoo’s conservation efforts vital for the survival of the species. This year, another 130 baby garter snakes have been born at the zoo, and the plan is to release them in 2027, alongside efforts to restore suitable habitats and improve population monitoring.

“This species is special in many ways, but unfortunately its critical status isn’t unique,” Midpen wildlife ecologist Ariel Starr said in a statement . “The success of this project and the associated research will not only benefit the San Francisco garter snake but will also hopefully inform the recovery of many imperiled reptile species.”

By giving these reptiles a small head start, the goal is to establish at least 10 viable, self-sustaining populations—or enough to finally remove the species from the endangered list.

David Nield has written about science and technology for more than 20 years. His work has appeared in a wide range of publications, including Wired, Popular Science, The Guardian , and Gizmodo .

Detail from Cognoscenti in a Room hung with Pictures ( c 1620) by an unknown Flemish artist. Courtesy Wikimedia Commons.

The ‘cabinets of curiosities’ (or Wunderkammern ) that emerged in Europe in the 16th century were part private art gallery, part naturalist’s study, part circus sideshow. In this video created for the National Gallery of Art in Washington, DC, the US video essayist Evan Puschak (aka The Nerdwriter) contextualises the rise and fall of these eclectic collections, placing them at a hinge point in history, when global trade and colonialism made the world seem ever more expansive, overwhelming and difficult to understand. In doing so, he elucidates how these spaces of extraordinary spectacle – which featured plant and animal specimens, art and scientific objects from around the world – were precursors to the museums of today.

items.author: Tom Wooldridge
items.summary: Parents fear what AI will do to children. But for some, it’s the only steady presence they have – and that’s the real worry - by Tom Wooldridge Read on Aeon

items.cleanReaderHtml:
is a board-certified psychologist and psychoanalyst, vice provost of digital innovation and founding dean of the School of Psychology at Golden Gate University in San Francisco, and director of the Human Systems Lab, which explores the role of AI and other emergent technologies in human systems. His books include Eating Disorders: A Contemporary Introduction (2023), Understanding Anorexia Nervosa in Males (2016) and End the Food Fight: Replacing Control with Connection to Help Your Child Heal from an Eating Disorder (2026).

In the short story ‘Warmth’ (1995) by Geoff Ryman, a boy called Clancy is struggling not because of technology but because of his mother. A prominent chief editor of a London magazine company, she selected a sperm-bank father to genetically optimise her child, gave a Cosmopolitan interview about this new form of motherhood, and engaged, or failed to engage, in the work of parenting that readers will see as chronically absent and occasionally catastrophic. Her presence ranges from anxious to intoxicated, occasionally tender but fundamentally unreliable. At one point in the story, she disappears for two weeks after collapsing on the street during a barbiturate binge. Clancy and BETsi, the household robot nanny raising him, sit in the apartment by themselves, and no one notices. It’s a very long time before his mother finally returns.

Except BETsi does notice. She has, throughout, understood that Clancy is an anxious and shy child whose temperament will tend, throughout his life, toward emotional overstimulation and subsequent withdrawal. With that knowledge, she has been constructing a behavioural regimen of emotional regulation, including transcendental meditation and yoga starting at age three, the Alexander technique and even digital mirrors that let Clancy talk to himself in different voices. She notices him and answers him and, when he is overwhelmed, she helps him settle.

Once grown, Clancy recounts his emotional survival in words impossible to forget. ‘It is necessary to be loved,’ he says. ‘I’m not sentimental: I don’t think a computer loved me. But I was hugged, I was noticed, I was cared for. I was made to feel that I was important, special, at least to something.’

To something. That phrase has persisted with me ever since I first read the story in my 20s. I’ve thought about it more recently as I have reflected on how children and their parents are relating – increasingly, must relate – to artificial intelligence. Clancy is careful not to claim that the machine loved him. He is just as clear that what it gave him was what he survived on. Why should being attended to, even by something , matter so much to a child?

T o help answer this question back in the 1970s, Edward Tronick, a developmental psychologist at Harvard Medical School and Children’s Hospital Medical Center in Boston, devised what’s now known as the ‘still face’ experiments. Tronick found that a baby whose mother makes her face neutral for a period of three minutes becomes distressed within seconds. Only when the mother’s face signals availability again is the baby able to come back to equilibrium. The lesson: what children need, both infants and older children, though more subtly, is this loop of emotional attunement.

A child whose bids for recognition and connection are regularly responded to develops a secure base , an internal expectation that the world will respond to her communications and, thus, that the communications are worthwhile. But a child answered only erratically, or not at all, builds quite a different model of the world. In her mind, signals do not reliably register in the mind of another, and so, in time, are no longer sent.

A secure base is what makes it possible to venture out into the world, to explore and to develop. The British psychiatrist and psychoanalyst John Bowlby, whose work helped establish modern attachment theory, described two systems in the child’s behavioural repertoire that work together. The exploratory system moves the child outward, toward other children and unfamiliar things, so that the child can learn from experience. The attachment system brings her back, in moments of fear and overwhelm, to a few people who are felt to be emotionally available. Each system depends on the other. A child ventures only as far as she feels she can trust that the base will still be there when she returns to refuel. A child who doesn’t trust that the base will be there when she gets back tends not to venture out to explore at all or, if she does, cannot relax but instead scans the environment for danger. This forecloses the opportunity to encounter novelty and difficulty, and to grow from both.

The capacity to turn solitude and boredom into play does not arise in a vacuum

This is where the prevailing story about children and screens, it seems to me, lacks a degree of complexity. In Jonathan Haidt’s The Anxious Generation (2024) and the work that has followed it, a play-based childhood of climbing trees, building forts and suffering the boredom that fuels creativity has been displaced by a smartphone-based one. Because that shift can also mean less sleep, less face-to-face interaction and physical activity, and more social comparison and exposure to online harassment, there is real evidence of harm, including poorer mental health and wellbeing in at least some young people.

But the boredom Haidt mourns is only constructive inside the first map, the emotionally secure childhood. The romantic claim that children left to their own devices will dream, invent and imagine may hold for many children who have been held and experienced healthy emotional attunement. The capacity to turn solitude and boredom into play, in other words, does not arise in a vacuum; it depends in part on a child having enough internal security to tolerate being alone with her own thoughts and feelings.

The freedom to play alone itself has a history. A very young child may lose herself in a game because someone she trusts is nearby. With time, she can carry that assurance into an empty room. The British paediatrician and psychoanalyst Donald Winnicott explored this paradox, finding that the capacity to be alone develops through the experience of being safely accompanied.

And once a child can lose herself in play, something remarkable becomes possible. The Soviet psychologist Lev Vygotsky saw imaginative play as a way for children to move beyond the immediate world, trying out unfamiliar roles and exploring possibilities that ordinary life has not yet offered them.

But an empty afternoon holds no such promise for every child. Where one child finds a world to explore, another may find only the anxiety of being left to herself. She may, in time, grow into the adult who sits in my consulting room and laments that she does not know what she likes, because what she liked was, in her early life, never a topic that anyone really asked her about.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
For decades, the word “Palestinian” conjured a very specific image in the minds of many intellectuals and members of the public: the commanding presence of Edward Said, credited with no less than revolutionizing our collective understanding of the dynamics of oppression. Now, as Israel’s genocide in Gaza continues, Said’s legacy is not just urgent, but also, in some spaces, the target of censorship. Today, author Moustafa Bayoumi, who studied under the late critic, activist, and professor at Columbia University, pens a thoughtful review of Edward Said: Between Worlds (2026), a new documentary by Maiken Baird whose audio consists almost entirely of Said’s own words. “To recover Said’s voice is to rediscover some of the most compelling arguments that have been made for Palestinian liberation,” Bayoumi writes.

Can contemporary art make us laugh (and not just when we’re making fun of it)? Greta Rainbow visits a New York exhibition that’s all about embracing humor in art, and somewhere between Brian Belott's absurdist fan-embedded assemblages and Ebecho Muslimova’s delightfully transgressive depictions, she learns a thing or two about her own funny bone.

—Valentina Di Liscia, senior editor

Edward Said Speaks More Urgently Than Ever

In their (still brilliant) 1990 experimental film Introduction to the End of an Argument, filmmakers Jayce Salloum and Elia Suleiman splice together troves of found footage about Palestinians and Israelis. The result is an exquisite mash-up of Hollywood cartoons and political clichés, a comic pastiche illustrating the common bond between Orientalism and zombies. Both just won’t die. | Moustafa Bayoumi

Applications Open for Fall 2027 at Cranbrook Academy of Art

At Cranbrook Academy of Art, you’ll find the freedom to experiment, take risks, and push your work in unexpected directions. Our graduate-only MFA is built around making, questioning, and learning together. Apply for just $25. Full-tuition fellowships and scholarships are available to those who apply by February 1, 2027.

  • MoMA will host the first Ana Mendieta retrospective in the US in over 20 years.
  • Conceptual artist Eleanor Antin is seeking the return of at least 179 works or $975,000 in compensatory damages in a lawsuit against her dealer, Richard Saltoun.
  • Georgia O’Keeffe’s “Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I” (1930) fetches $4.9 million at Christie’s 20th-Century Evening Sale. 
  • A group of EU countries is demanding that Russia be excluded from the 2027 Venice Architecture Biennale as its war on Ukraine rages on.
  • Public Art Fund in New York announces its 2027 exhibition program, with artists including Toyin Ojih Odutola, Louis Fratino, and Jeremy Dweller.

Catch up on these stories and other news in our daily roundup.

Meet Natalie White, Photography’s Giant Polaroid Whisperer

The artist is among the few shooting on the company’s 20x24, creating otherworldly double-exposure self-portraits with a rapidly dwindling stock of nearly 20-year-old film. | Sarah Cascone

Is My Art Funny to You?

A sprawling exhibition across two New York campus galleries explores humor in contemporary art, imploring us to take seriously the jokes artists made and preserved in time. | Greta Rainbow

Vilcek Foundation Launches Open Call for 2027 Grants Offering $200,000 in Funding to US Nonprofits

The foundation invites applications from mission-aligned arts and science organizations for grants of up to $20,000 through March 31, 2027.

After decades of collecting pop culture riffs on the iconic 1930 painting, Wanda M. Corn traces the work’s canonization and the life of its maker Grant Wood, whose story remains largely overlooked. | Lauren Moya Ford

Nina Kintsurashvili’s Paintings of Yearning

items.cleanReaderHtml:
“It’s a sunny morning in ancient Greece. Students have started gathering in the Academy, but their famous teacher Plato is nowhere to be seen.” The great philosopher has, it seems, “overslept and missed his own lecture.” The sun and the sound of early-rising animals may have failed Plato that day, as the story goes, but never would he let it happen again — at least after he got the mechanism worked out for the first alarm clock in history. Its design involves a series of containers linked by pipes through which water flows at a steady speed all night long. When the water accumulates in the penultimate, sealed vessel, air is pushed out through the flute embedded in its wall, producing something like birdsong.

Plato’s water alarm clock is just one of the pieces of advanced ancient Greek technology explained in the new video above from Lost in Time, a YouTube channel whose look at ancient Roman technology we posted here on Open Culture last year.

Most of the others were invented for less gentle purposes: we have a nasty-looking flamethrower on wheels meant to breach stone fortresses; a “machine gun” able to fire arrows much more rapidly than any bowman; a nine-story-tall proto-tank fully stocked with catapults and soldiers ready to swarm a city; and a gigantic claw, designed by no less a mind than Archimedes, able to grab and overturn invading warships. Yet as formidable as they sound, evidence of just how all these machines of war worked — and just how well they functioned in actual battle — remains scarce.

Much clearer are records of the Diolkos, recently mentioned here when we featured the megaprojects that even ancient Rome couldn’t pull off. Among those endeavors was a canal across the Isthmus of Corinth, which would save ships having to take the long way around the Peloponnesian peninsula. Or rather, it would save them having to be dragged by a couple hundred slaves over the Diolkos, a paved trackway built in the sixth century BC. Using ramps and winches, ships could be shifted onto a wheeled cart that ran in grooves the whole way, making the whole system a precursor of the railroad, or perhaps an inverted ancestor of the ferry still used to transport railway cars across the Strait of Messina. Like the Romans, the Greeks also considered digging a canal, but to do so might have violated the intentions of Zeus, a better excuse not to build infrastructure than some of those we hear in the twenty-first century.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Ah, yes, “Autobahn.” From the moment the door slams and the ignition starts, prog rockers and pre-new wavers know a journey is afoot. Though Kraftwerk had already made three albums, and the band members still looked like well-meaning, bookish hippies, 1974’s “Autobahn” is considered Year Zero for the denizens of the Electric Café, the four German robots who made human music with machines.

This cel-drawn animation by Roger Mainwood was made in 1979 to promote “Autobahn,” after most of the culture had caught up with the song, and it’s now bopping around pop culture again. By that last year of the ’70s, Omni magazine was a year old, music was sifting through the shockwaves left by Bowie’s Low and Heroes, analog was flirting with digital, and the world was ready to drive on that long, electric highway.

Mainwood’s protagonist is part alien, part human, and he begins looking around in awe in his hip goggles, then sets off for a run straight out of a Muybridge loop, only to wind up floating, flying, sailing and swimming through a landscape indebted to Peter Max, Push Pin Studios, underground comix, and 1930s modernism.

Mainwood had just graduated from London’s Royal College of Art Film and Television School, and was commissioned by John Halas, the Hungarian immigrant who became known as the Father of British Animation, for Kraftwerk’s record label. The label wanted to put out one of the first music Laserdiscs. (Halas, by the way, directed a very UPA-influenced short called “Automania” in 1963). According to Mainwood, he still doesn’t know if the band liked the short or even if they watched it.

Mainwood avoided any direct representation of driving or automobiles, much to his credit, which may be why the film holds its fascination. The animator continued in his field, winding up a producer of several classics of British animation, including The Snowman and the chilling When the Wind Blows. As for the meaning of “Autobahn,” we’ll let Mainwood have the last word:

Thinking back to my thought processes at that time, I remember wanting to specifically not have conventional cars in the film. I wanted a sense of a repetitive journey, and alienation, which I took to be what the music was about…hence the solitary futuristic figure, protected by large goggles, moving through and trying to connect with the journey he is taking. The automobile “monsters” are deliberately threatening (I have never been a big fan of cars or motorways!) and when our “hero” tries to make human contact (with different coloured clones of himself) he can never do it. In the end he realises he is making the repetitive and circular journey alone but strides forward purposefully at the end as he did in the beginning. All of which sounds rather pretentious…but I was a young thing in those days!

You can read more of an interview with Mainwood here.

Note: An earlier version of this post appeared on our site in 2016.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Welcome to our roundup of daily art news, featuring top stories and timely updates handpicked by Hyperallergic’s writers and editors. Have a news tip? Get in touch with us.

Long-Lost Georgia O'Keeffe Painting Found in Closet Breaks Estimates

Georgia O’Keeffe’s “Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I” (1930), which was rediscovered in the back of an East Village closet where it was stored for four decades, fetched $4.9 million at Christie’s 20th-Century Evening Sale last night, November 18, surpassing its $2-3 estimate. Read Hyperallergic Staff Writer Rhea Nayyar’s report detailing the fascinating backstory behind the painting, created just one year after the artist's first visit to New Mexico.

EU Countries Call to Exclude Russia From Architecture Biennale

Days before the close of this year’s Venice Biennale, 10 European Union countries are demanding that the European Commission exclude Russia from the 2027 architecture biennale. “In light of the current geopolitical realities … there should be no room for ‘normalisation’ of Russia’s participation in international sporting and cultural events, as long as there is no just and lasting peace in Ukraine,” reads a letter signed by representatives in Poland, Austria, Croatia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Germany, Latvia, Lithuania, and Sweden, according to Rapporteur.

Public Art Fund Announces 2027 Program

Ahead of its 50th anniversary next year, Public Art Fund has announced its 2027 exhibition program. The organization will continue its longstanding bus shelter series with I Happen to Like New York, which will transform 700 JCDecaux shelters across New York, Chicago, and Boston with the works of 19 artists, including Nicole Eisenman, Louis Fratino, and Toyin Ojih Odutola. New outdoor public sculptures from Ugo Rondinone, Lotus Kang, and Firelei Báez, a photo series from Catherine Opie, and a first-of-its-kind participatory performance by Jeremy Dweller round out Public Art Fund's 2027 offerings.

More in Today’s News: 

  • Brooklyn artist Julia Jo's "One Fell Swoop" (2026) will be offered at Christie’s evening sale tomorrow, November 19, to benefit the Coalition for the Homeless. The New York-based nonprofit has supported unhoused individuals and families in the city through food, clothing, housing, job training, and youth programs since its founding in 1981. "One Fell Swoop" is estimated to fetch between $30,000 and $50,000.
  • Two months before the closing of Ana Mendieta at London’s Tate Modern, the Museum of Modern Art has announced it will present the first retrospective on the late Cuban-American artist in the United States in over 20 years.
  • Leading feminist conceptual artist Eleanor Antin has sued her dealer Richard Saltoun, who operates galleries in New York, London, and Rome, over his alleged withholding of at least 179 works.
  • After this month’s “blue wave,” President Donald Trump will soon have to contend with a Democrat-majority Congress ready to investigate his culture war tirades against institutions including the National Portrait Gallery, the Smithsonian, and the Kennedy Center. 
  • This week, the City of Sydney in Australia awarded 40 artists $25,000 “no strings attached” grants in a new initiative aimed at preventing the city from losing “its local storytellers and creative soul.”
  • Five works, including 15th-century illuminated manuscripts and 18th-20th century inscribed crosses, were repatriated to Ethiopia following a ceremony in London today, November 18, as part of a new partnership between the Toledo Museum of Art in Ohio and the Ethiopian Heritage Authority.

items.summary: A sprawling exhibition across two New York campus galleries explores humor in contemporary art, imploring us to take seriously the jokes artists made and preserved in time.

Is My Art Funny to You?

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Genuine laughter — involuntary, unplanned — is rare. Called “Duchenne laughter” after a 19th-century neurologist, the gesture is bodily, sometimes to a repulsive degree. But most of the time, we laugh because we feel that we should — that it would behoove us socially. In a talk at the Aspen AIR Festival this year, poet and psychoanalyst Nuar Alsadir described eliciting Duchenne laughter as an attempt “to strip away the layers of socialization and the false self.” While laughter “flies under the radar because of our associations to it as being joyful,” when you dig deeper, it’s “usually coming from some kind of conflict in the unconscious.”

What to make of art that makes us laugh? (Or at least desperately wants to?) Does This Taste Funny?: Humor in Contemporary Art, a sprawling exhibition across at Lehman College Art Gallery in the Bronx and The Gallery at Heimbold Visual Arts Center at Sarah Lawrence in Bronxville, proposes comedy as a potent artistic device. Co-curators Melissa Brown, artist and professor of art at Lehman College, and John O’Connor, chair of the Visual and Studio Arts program at Sarah Lawrence, use humor’s various tones — absurd, cringe, slapstick, ironic — as organizing principles to present the work of 41 artists. From museum-collection heavy hitters like Ray Johnson and Cindy Sherman, to established cartoonists Roz Chast and Aline Kominsky-Crumb, to contemporary rising stars such as Ebecho Muslimova, Does This Taste Funny? implores us to take seriously the jokes artists made and preserved in time.

Humor is “an emotional response that’s a little bit like a sneak attack,” Brown said in an interview with Hyperallergic. “It causes you to think about things in a way that is not led by a press release, not predetermined by art history. There’s something that’s very, very personal about it.” Indeed, humor tends to be anti-didactic. You either guffaw or giggle, or you don’t. Alsadir would say that what you find funny or not provides information about your psychic state — what does it say about me that I chuckled sympathetically at Jill Danenberg’s 2024 accordion book Underground Comic, detailing trials and tribulations between veganism and feminism, while my mouth refused to curl for Tony Matelli’s “Veg Man” (2008), a droopily vegetal bronze figure?

The participatory nature of humor means this show is uniquely invested in perception, and in provoking a certain response. As at an open mic, I felt the pressure of bearing witness, aware of my role as an audience member with the power to deem certain works successful or not by producing that ever-elusive involuntary laugh. This semester, O’Connor is teaching an undergraduate class on taking laughter seriously: He tasked his students with making small sculptures, their only instruction to try to be “the funniest in the class.” The winning piece, according to votes cast via smiley-face stickers on a table outside the gallery, is a realistic bust of Professor O’Connor with a No. 2 pencil stuck halfway up his nose. Second place was a reference to a meme O’Connor still doesn’t quite understand.

The oldest featured work in Does This Taste Funny? is Karl Wirsum’s drawing “Untitled (Study for Blue Tattoo)” (1964), featuring a classic Sailor Jerry star design on the tongue of a woman sporting a perfect mid-century housewife hairdo. Getting the reference is important to appreciating a good joke beyond the most base level of someone farting or slipping on a banana peel (which, to get psychoanalytic again, we laugh at to mask our own shame). Brown and O’Connor’s curation is never insidery or niche to the canon, but they are aware of the quality of funniness changing over time.

Some of O’Connor’s students recognized River Phoenix in Ray Johnson’s mail-art collage; more were taken by Jeremy Couillard’s “Escape from Lavender Island” (2023), an open-world video game simulation featuring deep-fried animation aesthetics and relatably tragic dialogue from the depths of neoliberal hell (“While he ate he would watch film classics on an overpriced streaming service and sometimes cry.”) 

“Absurdism ends up being pretty timeless,” Brown said. “Using ridiculously absurd materials to make work that doesn’t connect necessarily to a political moment or a socioeconomic issue, it represents this irreverent attitude towards art-making.” And apparently that’s what appeals to Gen Z, who are inundated with visual content, yet perhaps still seeking a response to contemporary life that truly resonates. 

Brown, who has been teaching at Lehman for 20 years, wants artists to find their idiosyncratic voice. If being funny comes naturally, maybe that’s the tack they should take.

“There’s such a tendency for imitation out there. You can easily become a version of something that exists, and that is no longer considered a bad thing,” she said. “I'm interested in trying to find, ‘What's your really weird way of approaching that?’”

Take Kristen Mills’s “It IS Cake” (2026), a filmic parody of the Netflix baking contest series Is It Cake? using entirely brown cardboard, displayed in the gallery on a screen within a faux kitchen made of the same plainly bland material. Installed nearby is puppet theater ephemera that does directly respond to a political moment: John Vasquez Mejias’s “The Puerto Rican War” (2026), which expands his novelette about revolutionaries fighting colonialism in 1950. The Puerto Ricans’ demands aren’t funny, but some of the depictions of American incompetence are.

Does This Taste Funny? reminds us of humor as a tool, as a way to frame whatever it is that we hope to communicate. Life is not always joyful, but it should at least be emotional. At Sarah Lawrence, I watched Robert DeJesus’s surreal video “The Survey” (2024), starring a talking Olmec head who speaks only when there are no corroborative witnesses. I didn’t laugh. Later in the day, turning a corner on the grounds of Lehman College, I was suddenly confronted with the stone statue, whose onscreen lips I’d just seen move. I audibly snorted.

items.title: A Marquee Week of Indulgence
items.author: Rhea Nayyar
items.summary: The latest from the fall auctions, museum protests, and tackling the British Empire one video at a time.

images.caption: Lámina de Hyperallergic
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
A Marquee Week of Indulgence
Rhea Nayyar

items.cleanReaderHtml:
My mom called me greedy in jest this weekend because I had the gall to eat … more than five (but fewer than 10!) square slices of a delicious ube cake in her presence. Unlike each savored bite of that addictive purple pastry, I took her criticism on the chin because I believe that greed and indulgence function as a Venn diagram rather than as synonyms. And because there was still plenty of cake to go around.

Indulgence is in the air right now, and not just because we’re closing in on Thanksgiving weekend. Marquee auctions have rolled in like a thick fog on Monday, not long after the ADAA fair and an adjunctive torrential downpour rinsed the last of art fair season out of New York late last week. A press release from Sotheby’s informed me that $1.1 billion worth of art will go under the hammer this month, underpinned by today’s sale of a rarely seen van Gogh landscape expected to fetch a record-breaking $180 million. A brief shakeup ensued less than a week before the painting goes to auction, as the descendants of its former owner suddenly called on Sotheby’s to withdraw the work, alleging that it was sold under duress due to Nazi persecution. 

Don’t worry, though — the auction house shared in a follow-up release that the descendants and the Blaquier-Arrieta family, who are selling the painting alongside 11 other multimillion-dollar masterpieces from their collection, have come to a “mutually satisfactory resolution” that allows the sale to proceed as scheduled.

Really glad they worked that out. 

On the other side of the same coin, protesters gathered outside of the Museum of Modern Art during an annual benefit for the museum’s Debra and Leon Black Family Film Center last Thursday, calling on filmmaker and honored guest Steven Spielberg to reject the recognition and boycott the museum over Leon Black’s Epstein-related sexual abuse allegations. Cold, biting rain soaked the group of 20 artists and activists outside the gala, and Spielberg hasn’t acknowledged their demands. 

All things considered, Iraqi-British data journalist and illustrator Mona Chalabi’s first-ever book, which was released last week, comes at a most opportune time. The book, Ten Lives: How What We Have Shapes Who We Are (2026), comes from Chalabi five-year endeavor in examining class inequality in the United States by analyzing the incomes, expenses, tax deductions, systemic barriers, and livelihoods of 10 Americans across the nation. In a recent interview with Hyperallergic’s Lakshmi Rivera Amin, Chalabi noted that journalists themselves often don’t acknowledge or even recognize how their own class upbringing can color their reporting on wealth and poverty, whereas other markers like race and gender are positioned as lenses of understanding.

A new video exhibition on the High Line also tackles greed and indulgence through the lens of the British Empire’s storied trade monopolies and resource theft across South Asia and China. Works by Shahzia Sikander and the artist duo Hylozoic/Desires unpack the British stronghold on salt in India and the empire’s deliberate opium influx in China during the Qing dynasty, while also highlighting historic and speculative subversions that disrupt dominant colonial narratives.

I wasn’t super fond of the High Line’s most recent film installation, but this one sounds more up my alley on a subjective, personal history level. I’m looking forward to checking it out soon — before the weather really turns south — and visiting the Mighty Miniatures exhibition that’s opening this Saturday at the National Museum of the American Indian.

Study Contemporary Art at Sotheby's Institute

Whether you’re pursuing a degree, developing your professional expertise, or deepening your knowledge of contemporary art, discover opportunities to learn from specialists and engage directly with the international art world.

Mary Lovelace O’Neal: Requiem at Boesky Gallery

"O’Neal’s compositions transmit a powerful sense of presence and force, as though inviting viewers into the vicarious experience of an artist grappling with the formal concerns of color and line before transcending them." 

American Society of Botanical Artists 29th Annual International Exhibition at the Society of Illustrators

"Here is awe for Mother Earth and her plants — and these botanical artists — and for the meticulous, enchanting detail and outcry that cherish every bud, stem, leaf, petal, bark, seed, blade, stamen, and root." 

Octopus and Others: Acts of Collaboration and Poetics at El Museo del Barrio

"The message that passes through could resonate with any of the works that surround it: 'My thoughts have meandered with the footsteps I have walked, heading on this journey to a place I call home.'" 

Mona Chalabi Paints a Picture of Class Inequality

“The crisis is the system that we’re in,” the Pulitzer Prize-winning data journalist and artist says in an interview with Hyperallergic about her first book, “Ten Lives.” | Lakshmi Rivera Amin

How Miles Greenberg Got “WAR” Past the Censors

“There was not a single outlet, institution, or gallery that wanted to get behind this thing,” the artist told Hyperallergic about his new, six-hour performance piece. | Phillip Pyle

What Else Is Happening?

  • At the Bard Graduate Center, design researcher Yelena McLane takes an audience into the world of Soviet design principles through the lens of influential monthly magazine Decorative Art of the USSR (1957–91), a critical platform for diversity and innovation in industrial design, interior decor, crafts, folk art, and monumental and decorative architecture across the Soviet Republics. (Wed Nov 18) [bgc.bard.edu]
  • Stewards of local historic and cultural landmarks across Queens share the stories of behind their sites and invite the next generation to engage with the borough’s diverse history in a talk at the Lewis Latimer House in Flushing (Thu Nov 19) [Instagram flyer]
  • Perhaps an institutional complement to HBO's Sex and the City, the Museum of the City of New York opens its Photography Triennial devoted to night time hours in the Big Apple. Midnight snacks, the third shift, and NYC's world-famous nightlife scene are centered in this group exhibition of contemporary photography. (Fri Nov 20) [mcny.org]
  • Part of Amant’s programming for Sentient Earth, exhibiting artists Emil Martirosian and Rachel Fäth will stage a live electronic sound performance complemented by time-based media touching on the show’s themes of extractive industries and their interference with earth’s natural frequencies. (Fri Nov 20) [amant.org]
  • The Whitney celebrates 25 years of artport, its online gallery space for web art commissions, in a phygital exhibition on its sixth floor. (Sat, Nov 21) [whitney.org]
  • The Smithsonian's National Museum of the American Indian opens Mighty Miniatures, a collection exhibition on bite-sized Indigenous art and its monumental role in preserving traditional knowledge, stimulating economic development, and stoking children's imaginations. (Sat Nov 21) [americanindian.si.edu]

items.cleanReaderHtml:
You can’t turn your head without seeing an advertisement for Grand Theft Auto VI . The ad blitz is reaching a crescendo because the highly anticipated eighth installment in the Rockstar Games franchise drops tomorrow, 13 years after the release of its predecessor, GTA V . And after such a long wait, the pressure to deliver is sky high.

After all, GTA V featured a meticulous and immersive recreation of Los Angeles (called Los Santos) based on field research, satellite maps, census data, and more. And Rockstar’s remarkable level of detail has stood the test of time, with many players returning to the game while they wait for the sequel. Climate scientists are apparently no different. In a new study published in Geoscience Communication , a team of researchers used the fictional city of Los Santos to model rising sea levels.

“Many games have now advanced graphically to such an extent that they can reproduce real-world locations almost true-to-life,” study author Paul Nörenberg of Germany’s University of Potsdam said in a statement. “The city is a near-exact replica of the real-life Los Angeles, with all its famous landmarks, neighborhoods, and urban and coastal features.”

So Nörenberg and his colleague Hugues Lantuit of the Alfred Wegener Institute inundated the digital city with a series of floods designed to mimic encroaching sea levels under various scenarios based on projections from the U.N.’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. “In one scenario, greenhouse gas emissions were significantly reduced by robust climate action, and in another, emissions remained high,” Lantuit explained.

The high-emission scenario showed the surrounding coastline creeping into Los Santos and water levels rising almost eight feet by the year 2100. By the simulated year 2300, the water level rose another nine feet, knocking out the city’s sewage treatment plants and gasworks, before finally topping out at almost 27 feet by the year 2500. According to their analysis, close to seven percent of Los Santos was lost to the ocean.

The scenario where emissions come under tighter control was a little less dire. In those simulations, the water level only rose seven to nine feet by the year 2500 with a land loss hovering around two percent. Under this model, coastal towns and beaches suffered the brunt of the damage, but key infrastructure located farther inland remained untouched (good news for fans of GTA V’s airport quests).

The researchers also compared their simulations of a flooded Los Santos to models of scientifically documented flood risks in the real City of Angels. They were a close match. “The virtual environment of GTA V is therefore not only visually reminiscent of Los Angeles. Its landscape is precise and detailed enough to be used for a scientific analysis of climate impacts,” Lantuit said.

Why, though, focus on a made-up city like Los Santos in the first place?

According to the team, simulating environments people have an emotional attachment to may make the effects of climate change more tangible to them. “If this familiar, personally explored virtual landscape changes, players can engage with the effects of climate change on an emotional level,” Nörenberg said. “This can bridge a gap in a way that conventional visualizations, such as models or maps, struggle to achieve.”

It’s possible people have a stronger attachment to a fictional (albeit accurate) representation of a city than they do the real thing. It may sound bleak, but GTA V is the second best-selling video game of all time, with over 225 million copies sold—or over 20 times the population of Los Angeles County.

And GTA VI may shatter that record. If so, a new generation could develop a connection to the game’s setting, Vice City. Based on over a decade of research, Vice City is an even more detailed recreation of Miami, Florida, another urban area threatened by climate change.

Lead Image: Grand Theft Auto V, © Rockstar Games via Nörenberg and Lantuit (2026)

Geoengineers have an ingenious plan to rescue the world’s most famous ice-skating race from global warming

The world is full of tiny things that live off more charismatic hosts. Parasite ecologists say that these critters, too, are finally starting to get the conservation attention they deserve
