items.cleanReaderHtml:
This post is part of BHL at 20: Treasures from the Biodiversity Heritage Library , a series contributed by members of the BHL community, highlighting remarkable works from across the collection in celebration of its 20th anniversary.

The current iteration of the Field Naturalists’ Club of Ballarat (FNCB, or the Club) was established in 1952 and continues to thrive, with a healthy and active membership. Since it began, all being well, members have gathered for a monthly Club Meeting and excursion to sites of local natural history interest.

Of the 571 editions of The Ballarat Naturalist available online in the BHL at the time of writing, the December 2025 edition was selected for featuring in this “BHL at 20” Series.

Why? It showcases some of the most celebrated events and people in the Club’s history as events unfolded to bring them together.

Front cover of The Ballarat Naturalist , Dec. 2025 edition. Credit: Field Naturalists’ Club of Ballarat. View on BHL

There is no prerequisite of any specialist knowledge to join the FNCB, just a desire to learn more about nature and a willingness to be involved in efforts to ensure its preservation. Nevertheless, since its inception, FNCB has been most fortunate to benefit from the vast local knowledge of many notable amateur naturalists who have made exceptional contributions to the Club over many decades.

The most anticipated event on the FNCB’s annual Calendar of Activities is the Stella Bedggood Memorial Lecture. It was inaugurated in 1979 in honour of its late namesake in the year after her premature death to cancer. Mrs Bedggood was an outstanding amateur naturalist, self-taught botanist, conservation advocate, educator and photographer who held various offices in the Club including, most notably, the role of Secretary for 13 years.

Each year, the Lecture features a prominent speaker presenting a talk on a natural history topic relevant to the Ballarat region, often with a conservation thread as befits Mrs Bedggood’s legacy. In 2025, the Lecture was even more special for Club members than usual as it featured Roger Thomas who had just been announced as the winner of the prestigious Australian Natural History Medallion (ANHM) 2025. You can view a video recording of the event here .

The December 2025 edition of The Ballarat Naturalist features the write-up of Mr Thomas’s fascinating presentation titled: “ Ballarat’s Nature Noted: A retrospective of Nature writing over four decades ”. It showcased Mr Thomas’s 41 years of weekly “Nature Notes” articles in The Courier (Ballarat), which chronicled the turning of the seasons, special and unusual observations, threats to species and environments, the lifecycles of local flora and fauna, and trends in their abundance and distribution – a veritable gold mine of local natural history.

These introductions collated information from various sources, including the archive of “Nature Notes” articles penned by Roger Thomas for The Courier , historic editions of The Ballarat Naturalist , Dr Susan Kruss’s PhD thesis, A Voice for Nature: A History of the Field Naturalists Club of Ballarat (2024), and the Club’s nomination of Roger for the ANHM 2025.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Wildwood , set in a magical world in the unruly forests bordering Portland, Oregon, is the newest film from animation house Laika . Founded in 2005, the studio became acclaimed for its work on films such as Coraline (2009) and Kubo and the Two Strings (2016). Laika champions practical effects and stop-motion animation —a flipbook-like filmmaking style in which objects are moved frame by frame to create the action seen on screen. At 2 hours and 12 minutes, Wildwood is the longest stop-motion animated film ever made.

The story follows the courageous Prue and her classmate Curtis as she embarks on a fantasy adventure in the forests to find her kidnapped baby brother. Costume designer Deborah Cook developed more than 200 pieces for Wildwood .

After her work on Tim Burton’s Corpse Bride , Cook was approached by Laika to work on Coraline . “It was a definite yes,” she says of relocating her life from London to Portland to be part of what would become an Oscar-nominated film . After that production, she stuck with the studio. She was interested in how much Laika’s CEO Travis Knight, who directed Wildwood , was invested in stop-motion. “I really wanted to be part of that,” Cook says.

Wildwood is based on the 2011 middle-grade fantasy novel of the same name, written by Colin Meloy and illustrated by Carson Ellis.

In 2019, Cook got the Wildwood project and then the world shut down because of the Covid-19 pandemic the following year. Stuck in Portland, the city where the film would take place, the costume designer found herself exploring the region with a whole new set of eyes. All the while, Cook notes that she was “approaching this movie with a really fantastical element plus contemporary Portland.”

Ahead of Wildwood ’s October 23 release, Cook spoke with Smithsonian magazine about the knits and peacoats that she created to adorn the movie’s characters.

What were your first reactions to hearing the breadth of storytelling for Wildwood and the genres you’d pass through to tell the story in costumes?

It didn’t actually feel too daunting because I feel like it’s a reality that we live in Portland anyway. We work in an animation studio in the actual setting of Wildwood , so we live in that contemporary life in Portland, being aware of what everyone wears. It’s very much an outdoorsy kind of area. But then it’s also full of people with a real high level of imagination and creativity. So it felt like I was partway there to understanding that world already.

It was around 2020, literally the start of lockdown, and this was a fantastic anchor because it almost fit what was happening. I could go out to the end of my road and walk around the Wildwood Trail in Forest Park. That was our “permitted activity” to get outside. I saw so much more in the local nature of my environment than I’d ever really properly absorbed. That was fantastic, and the forest there is magnificent. It really felt quite Jurassic to me. The fact that over Covid, there weren’t as many park keepers meant it became more and more unkempt. Things were growing at a rapid rate and really uncontrollably—you could see that escalation weekly, which was magical in itself.

Walking around in the forest at that time, I was very aware of things that I was looking for to discover the vibe of our characters: Like, what would Prue and Curtis feel when they were walking around the forest? What would be normal to them? What would take them out of that world? What is the first thing you would see that would spark a sort of strange curiosity that there’s something mysterious happening that’s out of the ordinary?

Prue is wearing an everyday town coat to start with. She’s very buttoned up and tucked in. She has a few airs and graces, and she thinks she’s a little older and wiser than she is. But when it comes down to the nitty-gritty of having to go out there and rescue her brother, she switches to something that everyone was wearing at that time going into the forest. It’s a little more casual but practical; very, very pragmatic. Everyone has their clothes that would serve them well in a walk around the forest where any weather or climate might come their way. With her trusty boots and hair tied up, she became more of her true self. It revealed her soul a little more, revealing who she really was in a less guarded moment.

Wildwood takes place in a magical world around Portland. How did you begin to approach that world?

[Prue and Curtis] are going into this forest, and they’re seeing people they don’t recognize. They can’t read them very well. What’s been brought into that world is medieval armor, different ways of making clothing that people might have relied on even if there’d been a parallel civilization that we don’t know about. Where did that clothing come from? Was it left behind by previous civilizations?

There wasn’t anything that got into the impassable wilderness from our world. So it was very much fostering that thought process and understanding what could be in the impassable wilderness but also identifying what each different civilization might be wearing, like what those communities and citizens were wearing that identified them and made them separate from each other.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
This post is part of BHL at 20: Treasures from the Biodiversity Heritage Library , a series contributed by members of the BHL community, highlighting remarkable works from across the collection in celebration of its 20th anniversary.

The MBLWHOI Library’s BHL journey began in 2006 through contributing leadership, technical expertise, and hands-on librarian effort to the exciting BHL start-up period. Today and for many years, a quiet but deliberate process has taken place towards introducing grade school through graduate level students and researchers to the Biodiversity Heritage Library. This happens in a single one-hour-long class students attend in the MBLWHOI Library where BHL is presented as an online tool that students can learn to use to extend their research studies of bound paper science books and journals.

These classes use BHL content to show students (the youngest of whom nowadays have minimal experience using paper books) the look and tactile feel of books that are hundreds of years old, while referencing the BHL digital examples showing the interface of print and online in science publishing, such as bound-in-volume foldouts (foldouts are bound book pages sized larger than the size of the pages of a book and folded into the book). A quick foldout example is shown below, in a plate bound before the first page of volume 8, no. 81 (1672), Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London : An attempt of a new kind of telescope invented by Mr. Isaac Newton .

Part of the unique BHL and in-library viewing experience is looking at and being able to download and understand vital details, such as illustrations contained in foldouts. View in BHL .

The Marine Biological Laboratory (MBL) was founded in the village of Woods Hole, Massachusetts, in 1888 as America’s first private marine biological laboratory. In 1930, scientists at MBL and the nascent oceanography community collaborated in the founding of another of the key Woods Hole science laboratories, the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI).

In the 1870s, Spencer Fullerton Baird, Secretary of the then recently founded Smithsonian Institution followed through on a charge from US President Ulysses S. Grant to found the US Bureau of Fisheries. Through this process, Baird discovered that the regional waters surrounding the village of Woods Hole are particularly rich in marine biodiversity. This natural phenomenon is influenced by the mixing of warm Gulf Stream currents from the southeast with the cool Labrador currents of the northeast. Secretary Baird also realized that some of the strongest tidal currents on the East Coast of the US are located just off Woods Hole Harbor. See the historical note below from A biological survey of the waters of Woods Hole and vicinity , Sumner, F., Osburn, R., Cole, L. (1911) Bulletin of the Bureau of Fisheries v.31 p.12:

“… Many years ago, Woods Hole was selected by Prof. Baird as the most promising spot upon our coast for the commencement of a scientific study of fisheries problems. From the very outset he gathered about him a staff of naturalists of the type that was dominant in that generation — men eager to seek out every living thing concealed beneath the waves, to describe and figure and name…”

To this day we encourage students to explore the late-summer biodiversity of the waters surrounding Woods Hole by dropping a fishing line to explore the possible diversity of the catch.

On the wall of the office of the MBLWHOI Library is an 1873 poster that was originally hung in the classroom of the Anderson School of Natural History (1873–1875). This poster, with the quote below, was often attributed to Anderson School founder and Harvard professor Louis Agassiz. “Study nature, not books” was a statement reflective of learning through personal experience. The Anderson School of Natural History, which operated on Penikese Island near Woods Hole, was an antecedent of the Marine Biological Laboratory. This school was purposely sited on a postage-stamp-sized island so the students could do their work without summer seaside community distractions. The poster’s statement “Study nature, not books” is appropriate to the MBLWHOI Library and science study in Woods Hole because “learning science by doing science” is how research has traditionally taken place in Woods Hole. We tell the students attending the brief rare books class that we will revisit this quote later in the short class.

1873 poster, “Study nature not books”, from the MBLWHOI Library. Photo courtesy of the author.

In the MBLWHOI Library rare books collection, in Volume 1, number 8 (1666) of Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London , is an article titled: Directions for sea-men bound for far Voyages . Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London is considered the oldest continuously published scientific journal in the Western world. Its founding in the mid-1660s reflects efforts by scientists and science-interested people in Western Europe and the British Isles to create and document knowledge, compiling references to science experiments and meeting in person or through detailed correspondence to discuss often differing viewpoints on scientific matters. The journal articles which made up Philosophical Transactions were often letters received by the Royal Society, and the proceedings of meetings that took place at the Royal Society in London. Highlighted below are the first few lines of the article, Directions for Sea-men bound for far Voyages :

“It being the design of the Royal Society, for the better attaining the end of their institution, to study Nature rather than Books , and from the observations, made of the phenomena and effects she presents, to compose such a history of Her, as may hereafter serve to build a solid and useful philosophy upon…to think upon and set down Directions for sea-men going into the East- & West-Indies, the better to capacitate them for making such observations abroad, as may be pertinent and suitable for their purpose…”

Directions for Sea-men bound for far Voyages , from Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London , vol. 1, no. 8, p. 140 (1666). View in BHL .

Students can read on to see that article details are attributed to “Master Rooke”, Lawrence Rooke, a 17th-century English mathematician and astronomer from Gresham College in London. The article goes on to instruct “sea-men bound for far voyages” on what they should be doing to study nature hands-on, meaning: keeping a diary that would include using the instruments of the day to detail the data associated with their voyage: the compass, dipping needles, (another magnetic-field measuring device), visually taking note of the ebbing and flowing of the tides while noting ordinary and extraordinary events, mapmaking, depth measuring, to record and describe weather and astronomical observations, as well as filling and weighing bottles of seawater from different ocean depths.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Since long before the United States was formed, the continent has been the home of Native American people, including the Lakota, Navajo, Sioux, Cherokee, Apache, Dakota and others. The names of those tribes still designate our waterways (the Potomac River, Lake Erie), national parks (Shenandoah and Denali) and even some states (Michigan and Ohio). Native American communities have, of course, contributed more than geographical names and remain a vital part of the fabric of American life. About 7.4 million self-identified Native Americans live in the United States today, and many continue the rich and meaningful traditions of their heritage.

Jeff Campagna is a photo editor at Smithsonian magazine. You can follow him on Instagram at @jeffcampagna .

Tracy Scott Forson is a senior editor at Smithsonian magazine.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
This post is part of BHL at 20: Treasures from the Biodiversity Heritage Library , a series contributed by members of the BHL community, highlighting remarkable works from across the collection in celebration of its 20th anniversary.

With the world facing the dual crisis of climate change and biodiversity loss, the emergence of the Biodiversity Heritage Library (BHL) 20 years ago was timely. Over that 20-year span, BHL has grown to become “the world’s largest open access digital library for biodiversity literature and archives” 1 with a corpus of over 64 million pages. This vast corpus is also a repository of historical biodiversity data waiting to be extracted and used to inform a better understanding of anthropogenic effects on climate, the environment, and life on Earth.

Portraits of Walter Faxon taken at graduation from Harvard (1871) and later in life (1896). Harvard College; Heliotype Printing Co.

One “dataset” recently added to BHL is the Ernst Mayr Library ’s (EML) collection of Walter Faxon’s ornithological field journals , field notebooks and bird lists . Faxon (February 4, 1848 – August 10, 1920) was a native of Massachusetts. He was an Assistant Professor of Zoology at Harvard University from 1872 to 1886. Faxon specialized in the study of crustaceans and was Curator of the Invertebrate Department at Harvard’s Museum of Comparative Zoology (MCZ) for 46 years (1874–1920). He focused his work primarily on the Museum’s collections of Crustacea and Mollusca.

Pencil sketch of Pagurus sp. (hermit crab) first zoeal stage. Drawn by Walter Faxon on 3 August 1881. From the Ernst Mayr Library and Archives of the Museum of Comparative Zoology, Harvard University.

Ornithology was an avocation for Faxon, but he pursued it with the same level of professionalism with which he approached his curatorial work. He was a Fellow of the American Ornithologists’ Union from 1901–1904. “His long experience in the field [nearly 60 years] and his alertness of eye, ear and mind, as well as his scrupulous care to avoid error, combined to make him one of the best equipped and accurate of field ornithologists – the identification of a bird by him was never questioned.” 2 This inspires confidence in the authenticity of the historical data Faxon left for us, now accessible via the BHL.

The Faxon collection in the Ernst Mayr Library is relatively small, consisting of just over 2,200 pages of manuscript field journals, bird lists, field notebooks, correspondence, eight pencil drawings of Arthropoda and Crustacea, and some additional miscellaneous items. The EML also holds a large collection of William Brewster’s papers that include 145 letters to and from Faxon. Though not voluminous, Faxon’s field journals, bird lists and field notebooks (totaling 1,640 pages) record thousands of bird observations with species name, date, locality, number of individuals seen, and often additional information such as sex, life stage, and vocalization. These species occurrence data, compiled over 33 years (1886–1919), is arguably the greatest asset of Faxon’s collection. Aggregated with similar data from other sources around the world, the resulting dataset will help provide a clear picture of biodiversity change over time, informing efforts to mitigate accelerating species decline.

BHL is well positioned to facilitate development of an aggregated global dataset. By providing the infrastructure and tools to host transcript files for manuscript materials, making the text searchable and scientific names discoverable, BHL promotes extraction of species occurrence data.

With the goal of including Faxon’s data with BHL exports to the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF), the EML has digitized and transcribed his ornithological observations. In 2025, the collection was digitized with the support of the Harvard Library Collections Digitization Program under the theme of Climate Change. In 2026, the EML was chosen to host a Pforzheimer Fellow to investigate the use of AI-powered tools to transcribe Faxon’s field journals, notebooks, and species lists.

Our Fellow, Mohit Mandal , a Harvard PhD candidate in Anthropology, worked on this project from June 1 to August 31, 2026. He began by evaluating ChatGPT and Google Gemini to determine which model would be best suited for the Faxon materials. Mohit found Gemini to have the edge in accuracy, but more constrained by file upload limits and not as user-friendly, as it works only with Google Workspace tools (e.g., no support for Microsoft Word). He found ChatGPT to be more flexible with follow-up prompting and had success retaining consistency by training the model according to his specifications. Based on this assessment he chose ChatGPT for the project. The initial transcripts were then verified using a different AI tool, Claude, to draw upon the two models’ complementary capabilities and improve overall accuracy.

The screenshots below display page images alongside transcript text in the BHL book viewer. Overall, the results are impressive with pages reviewed thus far revealing relatively few errors. The goal of transcribing nearly 2,000 manuscript pages was achieved. The Pforzheimer Fellowship ended just one week before this writing, so we have not yet had time to calculate an accuracy metric. Some of the difficulties encountered are typical for transcription of handwritten material: notes written in pencil with smudges; marginal text written at an angle (poorly transcribed and, in some instances, not recognized by AI), etc.

One of the greatest challenges was training ChatGPT to capture tiny interlinear numbers and symbols that Faxon would place above the main lines of text (i.e., between lines). This interlinear text would record such things as the number of individual birds of a species seen on a given date, whether the birds were singing, and if they were in a flock. Mohit posits that the difficulty capturing this text may be a consequence of line-spacing constraints with word processors such as Microsoft Word and Google Docs. Ultimately, he was able to preserve the interlinear notations by formatting them as superscript text (Figures 3 and 4).

Left: Extract from Faxon’s April 1890 bird list highlighting his use of interlinear characters. Transcribed with ChatGPT-5.5 Thinking. From the Ernst Mayr Library and Archives of the Museum of Comparative Zoology, Harvard University. Right: Transcript of the extract with interlinear characters. ChatGPT would often miss these characters, especially on pages with difficult handwriting or on dates appended with more than one character. AI transcription of such characters requires further refinement.

Page 1 of Faxon’s Field Journal, v.1 (1889–91) , with transcript in BHL book viewer. Transcribed with ChatGPT-5.5 Pro. From the Ernst Mayr Library and Archives of the Museum of Comparative Zoology, Harvard University.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
This post is part of BHL at 20: Treasures from the Biodiversity Heritage Library , a series contributed by members of the BHL community, highlighting remarkable works from across the collection in celebration of its 20th anniversary.

As the Cataloging and Digital Resources Librarian for the Academy of Natural Sciences (Academy) of Drexel University , I get to work with a lot of different materials including periodicals, rare books, archival manuscripts, and more. I recently had the joy of working with scientists’ handwritten notebooks and field journals while completing a project to have 83 of them digitized and transcribed for BHL .

One of the selected notebooks stood out to me: A notebook containing an entomological essay by Carrie Aaron , in part because it highlights a common problem encountered when researching women in the natural sciences. Before uploading the notebook to BHL, the original finding aid record described Carrie as “Mrs. Aaron” and did not provide any additional information about her. Thankfully, Academy Archivist Jessica Lydon noticed the issue and provided more details for me to add to the record, leading me to build a BHL Creator ID for Carrie Aaron that links to her Wikidata identifier . This might sound like a small detail only librarians would notice, but it’s a huge step in building recognition for an author.

Page 1 of A notebook containing an entomological essay by Carrie Aaron, 1889, 1890, 1901 , Small Collections and Individual Manuscripts Box 4, ANSP-Coll-0156, Carrie Baily Aaron Papers, Library and Archives, Academy of Natural Sciences of Drexel University, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.

The updated catalog record provides more context around Aaron’s essay, which she submitted to a contest aimed at gathering information on how to eradicate mosquitoes. In Aaron’s written biographical notice about contest-holder Robert Henry Lamborn , she said, “While engaged in building the Lake Superior Railroad, Dr. Lamborn suffered so from the attacks of countless mosquitos, that he became interested in extermination of the insect, and later offered prizes for the three best essays on the subject.” I wonder if this was the motivation behind her essay submission.

With the help of dedicated Drexel University student digitization assistants, the Academy Library and Archives was happy to contribute the beautifully handwritten notebook to BHL, which showcases Aaron’s extensive entomological knowledge. Included are analyses of potential methods to reduce mosquito populations, including the use of dragonflies, which Aaron called “the hawks of the minuter insect world.”

A page from Carrie Aaron’s notebook on BHL in which she refers to hammer-headed dragonflies as “the hawks of the minuter insect world”. ( A notebook containing an entomological essay by Carrie Aaron, 1889, 1890, 1901, Small Collections and Individual Manuscripts Box 4, ANSP-Coll-0156, Carrie Baily Aaron Papers, Library and Archives, Academy of Natural Sciences of Drexel University, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.)

Aaron and her researchers apparently even attempted to inoculate themselves with what was then described as poisonous droplets from mosquitoes, but the attempt was “not successful, owing probably to the inferiority of the needle as an injector, compared with the delicate hypopharynx.” The essay was later published with other submissions in Dragon Flies vs. Mosquitoes: Can the Mosquito Pest be Mitigated? under the title “The Dipterous Enemies of Man.”

In addition to the essay, Aaron’s notebook in the Academy’s collection contains a letter from Henry Skinner congratulating Aaron on her prize-winning essay and confirming that her entomological reputation would “now be well established.” Ten years after receiving the congratulatory letter, Aaron wrote to Skinner in 1900 asking that her name be removed from the list of associate members of the American Entomological Society: “During the ten years of my membership I have attended only two meetings; this has not been from lack of interest as much as from the fact that lady members are too greatly in the minority, and also that I care so little for the classification of insects.” This is not to say that Aaron was not grateful to Skinner for their “more than thirty year sympathetic friendship,” for which she thanked him in a letter she wrote in 1923 .

Carrie Aaron asking that her name be removed from the list of associate members of the American Entomological Society. (Carrie Aaron letter to Henry Skinner, January 11, 1900, Box 1, Folder 1, ANSP-Coll-0150, American Entomological Society correspondence, Library and Archives, Academy of Natural Sciences of Drexel University, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.)

When given the opportunity to write a blog post in celebration of BHL’s 20th anniversary, it was an easy choice among the Academy Library and Archives staff to write about Carrie Aaron. The timing couldn’t have been better; shortly after choosing our blog post topic, we welcomed intern Will Le , who is currently digitizing our entire American Entomological Society (AES) correspondence collection , including letters written by Aaron, and uploading it to PA Photos and Documents . Funding for this project was generously provided by Dr. William Day and the American Entomological Society. Shout-out to Will Le, Jessica Lydon, Greg Cowper, and the American Entomological Society for making this happen!

Thanks to our intern and the AES digitization project, I was able to read Carrie Aaron’s letters on my laptop and learn about her travels in Santa Monica, a place she describes as “the land of perpetual bloom and uninterrupted sounds of birds and insects.” Later in this letter, Aaron describes a meaningful experience while visiting museums:

At Avalon we met the only woman curator of marine objects in the world and because she noticed how interested I was, also inquisitive, she shared a willingness to dissect and classify me; her museum contained many natural curiosities found in the waters of that locality. The most interesting museum I have ever seen is in Los Angeles, Exposition Park (of 130 acres) owned by the state, the resources and industries of California are shown in most attractive scenic effects. The exhibit of fossil remains of prehistoric animals really is wonderful, and made me regret not being healthy enough to make our Academy of Nat. Sci. a competitor in ownership of such a valuable contribution to scientific knowledge.

Aaron describes meeting “the only woman curator of marine objects in the world.” (Carrie Aaron letter to Henry Skinner, March 8, 1926, Box 1, Folder 1, ANSP-Coll-0150, American Entomological Society correspondence, Library and Archives, Academy of Natural Sciences of Drexel University, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.)
